value.question: What does NASA mean by systems engineering, and what broad activities does the discipline cover?

steps.description: Search the NASA document corpus (e.g., NASA Systems Engineering Handbook) for NASA's explicit definition of systems engineering
Identify the broad activities/phases the discipline covers, such as requirements definition, design, verification and validation, and technical management processes
Cross-check NASA's published systems engineering definition and activity scope on nasa.gov for corroboration

key_findings: NASA's SE handbook is intended to provide general guidance and information on systems engineering useful to the NASA community, and it "provides a generic description of Systems Engineering (SE) as it should be applied throughout NASA," with a goal of increasing awareness and consistency across the Agency and advancing the practice of SE (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p11-chunk-28; nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p10-chunk-27).

The handbook presents NASA-specific perspectives and data and is positioned as a companion for implementing NPR 7123.1, Systems Engineering Processes and Requirements, as well as Center-specific handbooks and directives developed for implementing SE at NASA (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p11-chunk-28; nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p10-chunk-27).

The only concrete activity coverage in the evidence sits in a program/project life-cycle and preliminary design context: estimating cost and range and developing a system-level cost-effectiveness model, defining the WBS, developing SOWs, and acquiring systems engineering tools and models, along with solidifying system requirements, top-level system architecture, and ConOps and developing conceptual designs and analyses (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p34-chunk-120).
gaps: No explicit definitional statement of what NASA means by systems engineering is captured: the Section 1.1 Purpose text breaks off mid-sentence ("It provides a generic description of Systems Engineering (SE) as it should be applied throughout NA..."), so the scope statement itself is not in evidence (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p10-chunk-27).

The evidence does not enumerate the broad activities/process areas the discipline covers; no list of SE processes or technical management activities is present, and the content of NPR 7123.1 is only referenced, not described (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p11-chunk-28).

Coverage of the life cycle is fragmentary and limited to Phase A/preliminary design excerpts; Pre-Phase A through operations, cross-cutting technical processes, and Center-specific variations are not documented, and one chunk is largely a contributor list (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p10-chunk-27; nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p34-chunk-120).

The evidence does not support the task's hierarchical pattern beyond handbook purpose and a partial life-cycle excerpt sequence; no parent/child structure of SE activities or sub-activities can be reconstructed from these three chunks.

value.text: NASA's Systems Engineering Handbook is intended to provide general guidance and information on systems engineering useful to the NASA community, giving "a generic description of Systems Engineering (SE) as it should be applied throughout NASA" and seeking to increase awareness and consistency across the Agency and advance the practice of SE. It is a companion for implementing NPR 7123.1, Systems Engineering Processes and Requirements, plus Center-specific handbooks and directives. On activities, the evidence covers only life-cycle and preliminary design work: cost estimation and a system-level cost-effectiveness model, defining the WBS, developing SOWs, acquiring SE tools and models, and solidifying system requirements, top-level architecture and ConOps with conceptual designs and analyses. The evidence does not state NASA's explicit definitional wording or enumerate the discipline's process areas, so the full hierarchical scope cannot be reconstructed.

issues: The activity 'cost estimation' is reconstructed from a truncated evidence fragment ('t estimate and range'), a small but acceptable extrapolation from the recorded text.
The answer's treatment of the 'broad activities' half of the question is thin relative to the hierarchical pattern, though it transparently flags the evidence gap rather than inventing process areas.

The handbook is positioned as a companion for implementing NPR 7123.1, Systems Engineering Processes and Requirements, together with Center-specific handbooks and directives.

The only concrete activity coverage in evidence is life-cycle/preliminary-design work: cost estimation and a system-level cost-effectiveness model, WBS definition, SOW development, acquiring SE tools and models, and solidifying requirements, top-level architecture and ConOps.

No explicit definitional statement of systems engineering and no enumeration of process areas (requirements, design, verification and validation, technical management) appear in the evidence, so the hierarchical activity structure cannot be reconstructed.
